intent: Have two bounded contexts co-own a small, explicitly shared piece of the domain model — kept tiny, gated and tested together — so that shared concepts have exactly one definition.
problem: Two contexts need the same concept (an identifier, a value type, a rule) and each defines it separately; the two definitions drift, reconciliation becomes a recurring bug, and the alternative — translating between two near-identical models — costs more than the coordination.
context: The shared kernel sits between partnership (which costs coordination time) and separate ways (which costs duplication). It is a genuine overlap of the two models, not a shared utility library: common utility classes alone do not make a shared domain model. It is appropriate only when the duplication cost exceeds the coordination cost — when the two contexts are tightly cohesive, when geography or politics block a partnership, or when contracts are held by the same team. Keep it small, require joint sign-off on every change, and gate it with integration tests and continuous integration. If the kernel grows faster than it stabilises, split the contexts and downgrade the relationship.
benefits: Shared concepts have one definition, so there is nothing to translate between the two contexts.
Both teams release the same contract, which removes a whole class of version-skew defects.
The coordination cost is bounded because the kernel is small and explicitly co-owned.
Both contexts inherit the same rules, so the model stays consistent across the seam.
Cheaper than an anti-corruption layer when the two models genuinely overlap.
tradeoffs: Every change to the kernel requires agreement from both teams, by construction — neither can release independently of the other.
The kernel tends to grow: it is the easiest place to put something that "belongs to both", so it becomes a dumping ground.
It contradicts one-team-per-context, so it needs an explicit organisational commitment.
Common code shared without shared semantics is just duplicated liability, not a shared domain model.
If the overlap is smaller than expected, the coordination overhead exceeds the duplication it saved.
quality_attributes_note: type_safety 8 because a shared type is shared statically. extensibility 5 and simplicity 5 because the kernel constrains both sides. reliability 8: one definition removes drift.

participants.responsibility: The small overlapping region of two models, co-owned and gated.
participants.notes: Keep it to integration contracts and shared data structures; shared rules are allowed only if both contexts agree to share them.

participants.responsibility: The part of the domain model both contexts genuinely share.
participants.notes: If it holds only utility code, it is not a shared domain model.

participants.responsibility: Own the kernel jointly; each change needs mutual agreement.
participants.notes: Evans: a shared kernel is a small, common model both teams keep in sync.

participants.responsibility: The gate that fails when the kernel and its consumers diverge.
participants.notes: Continuous integration is a precondition for the pattern, not a follow-on.

use_cases: Sharing an `AccountId`, `Money` and `OrderState` value-type library between two contexts owned by one team.
Sharing a schema fragment that both contexts read as the contract between them.
A temporary arrangement during a legacy modernisation where both contexts must agree exactly.
Two contexts whose ubiquitous language is deliberately identical over a narrow area.
avoid_when: The contexts are owned by teams in different organisations with no negotiation channel.
The overlap is a handful of constants — that is duplication, cheaper than coordination.
The kernel would contain shared business rules that only one context actually applies.
Either team changes weekly; the coordination cost then exceeds any duplication saving.
pitfalls: The kernel becomes a dumping ground and both "independent" contexts can no longer release separately.
Sharing utilities and infrastructure rather than domain semantics, calling it a shared kernel.
One team unilaterally changing the kernel and informing the other afterwards.
Assuming "shared" means "read-only" — read-only is not enforced, and it is what makes the kernel grow.
Letting the kernel grow faster than it stabilises instead of splitting the contexts.

related_patterns_notes.context-mapping: Shared kernel is one typed edge on the context map, sitting between partnership and separate ways in cost.
related_patterns_notes.partnership: Partnership coordinates the teams; shared kernel coordinates the model. Use shared kernel when the overlap is real but the coordination must be structural.
related_patterns_notes.separate-ways: The deliberate opposite: pay duplication instead of coordination.

anti_patterns: A `common` or `shared` library with no domain semantics, collected over time.
A shared ORM base class or shared persistence schema used as the kernel.
A kernel that both teams can modify without coordination.
Duplicating the shared types "temporarily" and keeping both copies for years.
Sharing a large fraction of both models, which means the contexts are not really separate.
design_principles: Keep the shared kernel small — the smaller it is, the cheaper the coordination.
Every change to the kernel requires agreement; this is the price of the pattern.
Use it only when duplication cost exceeds coordination cost.
Gate every kernel change with integration tests and continuous integration.
A shared kernel is a shared domain model, not a shared utility library.
best_practices: Put the kernel in its own artifact (library or schema package) with a named owner on each side.
Require joint sign-off in the merge process, not by convention.
Review the kernel regularly: if it keeps growing, split the contexts and downgrade the relationship.
Keep shared rules in the kernel only where both contexts genuinely apply them.
Version the kernel and upgrade both consumers together — the pattern exists precisely so skew cannot happen.
Name the kernel after the domain concept it shares, not after the team or the project.
